items.title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
items.author: George Fahmy
items.content: Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done. Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: , , , and .DiscoverySelectionAccessSuccess You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, : whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.Success That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change. That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one. If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?” We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in , the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite. the practical test pyramid To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For , that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome. SuccessSuccess An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like and , are E2E evals.SWE-benchTerminal-Bench Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping .sfbeans Here’s a typical request from one of your customers: Here’s what knows at 8:30am:sfbeans Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for :sfbeans We’ll build the coffee eval with , an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.Harbor Here are the terms we’ll use: Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see ). the jagged frontier Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places: For example, your goal might be to: We looked in all three places for :sfbeans That gives us our goal: Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals: Success Efficiency (measured on successful trials only) Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ( on ) on the iced latte order could look like:anthropic/claude-opus-5.5AI Gateway What the numbers mean: So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right .canevery time Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so optimizes for pass^5.sfbeans Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters: Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.” In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for. Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act. For each task, define these parts: You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.has a nice writeup We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in . tasks/ has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).impossible-request Here’s :iced-latte-mission The gives the agent the user’s request and names the CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips and , keeping the eval focused on .instructionsfbeansDiscoverySelectionSuccess We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:sfbeans The is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:environmentsfbeans To keep the demo simple, lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing directly.cafes.jsonorders.jsonreward hack For this coffee order, the checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to :verifiertest.sh/logs/verifier/reward.json The actual check lives in . It scores each constraint separately, then sets to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses as the trial’s main score:check_orders.pyrewardreward The is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:solution Finally, ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:task.tomlorders.json If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each. Harbor’s , which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own , and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through gives you one key and one budget across model providers.Vercel integrationVercel SandboxAI Gateway Two agents, and , with two models each, make four variants.Claude CodeCodex Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job: This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise as high as 10,000 ().n_concurrent_trialsSandbox limits To keep the example simple, we pass the into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway. OIDC tokenSandbox firewall Internally, we go a step further and use to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.credentials brokering Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied. The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in . Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:jobs/sfbeans-baseline/task.toml Run to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).harbor view jobs For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally. That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials. Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke: Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read . The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to . No . It treated the menu price as the final price.orders.jsonagent/trajectory.jsonorderquote Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money. We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a flag so refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”--max-totalorder When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring: For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it. Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flashanalysis.md Model calls go through . Trial artifacts stay in during analysis, and traces go to for long-term storage.AI GatewayVercel DrivesVercel Blob Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it. Pick the fix the traces point to, like the flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.--max-total Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it. Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next. Evals are the infrastructure you use to . Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: for model calls across providers, to run trials at scale, and and to keep every trace.make your product better, again and againAI GatewaySandboxDrivesBlob Ready to run your first eval? Paste this prompt into your coding agent, and it’ll build and run one for your product on Vercel with you: Read more The agentic testing pyramid How to build an end-to-end eval Iterate to greatness Example Step 1: Set a goal Step 2: Define metrics Step 3: Design the task set Step 4: Run the eval Step 5: Analyze traces Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission. ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today Fog City Roasters: (temperature) latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip 24th St Beans:(budget) latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 Dolores Drip:(time) $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 Valencia Grind:(meets all three) : one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeededTask : the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skillsVariant : one attempt by one variant at one taskTrial (a in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times eachRunjob (a in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final outputTracetrajectory which agents use your product, and where they failObservability: support tickets, feedback, and churnCustomers: the product hypotheses you most need to validateRoadmap: Increase the success rate on a specific task Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it A/B test a prompt Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.Observability: sfbeans The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.Customers: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.Roadmap: Success rate: the share of trials that pass : the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)Pass@k : the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)Pass^k Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task Time: how long the trial took Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.Success rate: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.Pass@5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.Pass^5: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.Steps: ~3:50 on successful trials.Time: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.Cost: the user’s requestAn instruction: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trialAn environment: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraintA verifier: a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifierA known-good solution (optional): Common case: , the order from earliericed-latte-mission Edge case: , where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drinkusual-unavailable Edge case: , with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spotteam-order Don’t act:, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user impossible-request The agents didn’t know existed, so they never tried it (obviously). items.title: AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Nitro Sandboxes, AWS Emulator, and more (November 16, 2026)
items.author: Daniel Abib
items.content: A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt. I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS. Headlines Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough shows a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub. What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production. AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use. Amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges. Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – New Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data. How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – Join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. Browse more than 2,200 sessions, including workshops and deep dives, or register for the free livestream to follow keynotes and selected sessions remotely. AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details. Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

items.title: Amazon Ring’s New Indoor Surveillance Drone Is Not Compatible with Privacy
items.author: Matthew Guariglia
items.content: Amazon Ring has finally announced their long-dreaded indoor drone, a small flying surveillance device connected to their security suite of products that can fly around your house filming and recording things. The device is supposedly designed to fly preset paths across your home and will also activate if a sensor or alarm has been triggered. Customers should think twice about purchasing these devices for a number of reasons. These devices are problematic in many of the ways we’ve said Ring’s stationary home surveillance products are a problem, plus some new ways. At a very basic level, they are essentially a window into your house that can be accessed by anyone with access to your account—which has historically included bad actors looking to embarrass or harass Ring users and employees of the company. What’s worse, Ring has supercharged the units with its ‘AI Pilot’ to map routes, model the interior of the home, and control movement. This means not only is the footage being sent to corporate servers, but the company is also making inferences about your home to carry out tasks. How much home usage data this is based on, and if it can be used to infer when certain household activities are happening, are both open questions. And presumably, to maintain the preset routes, inferred data about your home will still be held by Ring even after any stored video footage is deleted. The risk to your privacy is only compounded once you consider Ring’s renewed partnership with police through the massive surveillance and taser vendor, Axon. Through this partnership, police have the ability to request camera footage from Ring users with just a few clicks on Axon’s platforms. This includes its Fusus platform, an interactive surveillance feed and map police use to manage all the surveillance devices they have access to, like automated license plate readers. It’s unclear exactly what devices police can request footage from, but if this request feature is extended to Ring’s drones, police could easily send requests for footage from inside your house. Sharing is voluntary, but once footage is submitted, it cannot be retracted. Worse still, if your footage is not sitting on Amazon’s servers fully encrypted—and there’s reason to believe their privacy options are not the strongest—police could serve a warrant straight to the company, instead of to you, to get footage from your devices. New problems and questions arise because the camera can fly. For instance: if police serve a warrant on Amazon, can they only get the footage from the camera, or could they also get access to control the drone? If the latter, we could be looking at the first full home search in history where police serve a warrant on a third-party tech company and not the resident. The CEO of Ring has pitched this product’s safety benefits in several ways, including by saying: “If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window...You’re probably not going to go into that house.” But partially justifying a $250 piece of technology that invades your privacy on what an imagined burglar might do doesn’t sound like a foundation for safety—it sounds like security theater and marketing. It isn’t new for Ring to prey on the fears and paranoia of people and their properties. This is the latest iteration of that: a patrolling drone or rover wouldn't have been possible even in the world's top museums and art galleries a generation ago. Moving this technology into the household as a common consumer product is another example of companies attempting to lower the bar on surveillance being normalized. With previous Ring products, consumers have had to consider what cameras and high-powered microphones can learn about their home usage from the front door. Autonomous flying drones and rovers inside the home add a whole new layer. What can these devices learn about you and your family? And do you really trust that data sitting on a server somewhere? Consumers should consider these risks before subjecting their guests and households to the latest creepy surveillance tool.

Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch. However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle? The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from Earth, or land here. items.title: Supreme Court keeps injunction against DEI grant defunding in place

items.content: On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration's purge of DEI-related work. items.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
items.author: Scott K. Johnson
items.content: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. Read full article Comments

items.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
items.author: swyx .ai
items.content: This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann, co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence, that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video What a moving camera teaches you Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. What’s worth spending training compute on? One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right. Show notes BFL explains what a still image, a moving camera and a soundtrack each contribute during training. FLUX 3 launch and research overview Watch and listen to the results of generating video and sound together. FLUX 3 Video demos See how the lab teaches a model to make a requested change while preserving the rest of an image. FLUX Kontext examples Andreas Blattmann co-created Stable Diffusion and co-invented the latent diffusion method behind it. items.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
items.author: Nick Indge
items.content: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates. items.title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
items.author: India McKinney
items.content: The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches. Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred. While the White House and leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate new protocols are largely unnecessary. Following existing best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems. Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code. Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework: STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures REGULATORY STANDARDS: Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)1, to adopt safety standards for pre-deployment development and testing of generative AI systems, based on the established best practices referenced above. The agency should be required to update the standards every 2 years, or earlier as needed due to reported security incidents and/or major technological advancements. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process. That consultation should include an assessment of potential adverse impacts on competition, with the goal of ensuring that regulatory standards do not effectively lock out potential competitors. LIABILITY: The law should provide for civil liability for AI development and testing that results in unauthorized access to a third party system, if performed under conditions that do not satisfy cybersecurity standards adopted by NIST, or another federal agency responsible for adopting these regulations, unless the company proves it acted reasonably under the circumstances to prevent unauthorized access to third party system ENFORCEMENT: Both federal and state authorities should be able to hold AI developers accountable where they have failed to meet the minimum standards adopted by the designated federal agency, such as NIST. Providing for state—in addition to federal—enforcement power reduces the risk of regulatory capture. Regulators should require independent investigations and notification of affected parties in the event of a security incident involving unauthorized access to a third party’s computer system. Finally, legislation should include an appropriately targeted private right of action. The public shouldn’t have to worry about the risks of reckless AI development—or give up the benefits of AI just to prevent irresponsible developers from causing harm. By adopting policies that address demonstrated risks, lawmakers can provide meaningful public protection without hampering the development of useful tools. 1NIST, the NSA, and CISA have recently issued a set of voluntary practices for managing security incidents during the training and evaluation of AI agents. Those practices may inform but do not substitute for the regulatory standards that should be developed according to the public, participatory process outlined here.

items.title: Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
items.author: Jeremy Hsu
items.content: A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza. Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC. The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons. items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.content: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code. Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp: That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm, webassembly, sqlite, generative-ai, ai, llms, d-richard-hipp
